title: Freytag v. Commissioner (1991)
summary: Special trial judges of the Tax Court are inferior officers, and the Tax Court may appoint them because it is a Court of Law under the Appointments Clause.
notes:
Key line: The Clause reflects our Framers' conclusion that widely distributed appointment power subverts democratic government. (Justice Blackmun)

Citation: 501 U.S. 868 (1991).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were Thomas Freytag and other taxpayers who had invested in a tax shelter program and faced federal income tax deficiency determinations totaling about $1.5 billion. The respondent was the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, who had issued the deficiency notices. The decisionmaker whose status was contested was Special Trial Judge Carleton D. Powell of the United States Tax Court, appointed by the Chief Judge of that court under 26 U.S.C. section 7443A. Kathleen M. Sullivan argued for the taxpayers, and Deputy Solicitor General John Roberts argued for the Commissioner. Former Solicitor General Erwin Griswold filed an amicus brief.
sections.Material Facts: Congress created the Tax Court as an Article I court in the Tax Reform Act of 1969. It has nineteen judges appointed by the President with Senate consent for fifteen-year terms. Section 7443A lets the Chief Judge appoint special trial judges and assign them declaratory judgment proceedings, small cases and deficiency cases under $10,000, and, under subsection (b)(4), any other proceeding the Chief Judge designates. Petitioners' cases were assigned in March 1982 to Judge Richard C. Wilbur. Trial began in 1984. Judge Wilbur fell ill in November 1985, and the Chief Judge assigned Special Trial Judge Powell to preside as evidentiary referee with the proceedings videotaped. When Judge Wilbur took senior status on April 1, 1986, the cases were reassigned to Powell under (b)(4) with petitioners' consent. Powell's opinion went against petitioners, and the Chief Judge adopted it as the opinion of the Tax Court.
sections.Procedural History: Petitioners lost in the Tax Court after the Chief Judge adopted Special Trial Judge Powell's opinion. They appealed to the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, arguing for the first time that section 7443A(b)(4) did not authorize assignment of large complex cases to a special trial judge and that, if it did, the appointment of special trial judges by the Chief Judge violated the Appointments Clause. The Fifth Circuit rejected both arguments and affirmed, 904 F.2d 1011 (1990). The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on April 23, 1991, and decided the case on June 27, 1991. It affirmed. Justice Blackmun wrote for a unanimous Court in Parts I through III and for five Justices in Part IV.
sections.Issue: Two questions were presented. First, does section 7443A(b)(4), which lets the Chief Judge assign any other proceeding to a special trial judge, reach complex deficiency cases involving over a billion dollars, or is it limited to minor matters? Second, if the assignment was authorized, does the appointment of special trial judges by the Chief Judge of the Tax Court satisfy the Appointments Clause of Article II, section 2, which allows Congress to vest the appointment of inferior officers only in the President, the Courts of Law, or the Heads of Departments? Answering the second question required deciding whether special trial judges are officers at all and whether the Tax Court is a Court of Law or the Head of a Department.
sections.Holding: The statute authorizes the assignment. Subsection (b)(4) contains no limiting words, and neither the structure nor the history of section 7443A restricts it to small or simple cases. The appointment is constitutional. The Court exercised its discretion to reach the structural claim despite petitioners' consent to the assignment. A special trial judge is an inferior officer, not an employee, because he holds a continuing office established by law and exercises significant authority, including independent decisional power in (b)(1) through (b)(3) cases. The Tax Court is not a Department, because that term means executive divisions like the Cabinet departments, but it is a Court of Law within the meaning of the Clause, so its Chief Judge could appoint special trial judges. Judgment affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Blackmun read the words any other proceeding according to their plain meaning and found nothing in the statute's history to cut them back. Turning to the Constitution, he stressed that the Appointments Clause is a structural safeguard, so the Court would hear the challenge even though petitioners had consented to the special trial judge. Special trial judges are officers under Buckley v. Valeo and United States v. Germaine: their office is created by statute, their duties, salary and means of appointment are fixed by law, and they take testimony, conduct trials, rule on evidence and enforce discovery orders, exercising significant discretion. The Clause prevents Congress from diffusing the appointment power too widely, which the Framers thought would subvert democratic government. Because the Tax Court is not the President, the appointment must come from a Court of Law or a Head of Department. Germaine limits Departments to executive divisions like Cabinet departments; treating every executive organ or an Article I court as a Department would multiply appointing actors and defy Congress's intent in making the Tax Court a court rather than an executive agency. Courts of Law, however, are not confined to Article III courts. Congress may create legislative courts, and a body that exercises judicial power exclusively, as the Tax Court does with review in the courts of appeals like a district court, is a Court of Law able to receive the appointment power.

topics.lrs-s-officer-employee: A continuing legal office carrying significant adjudicative discretion made special trial judges officers.
topics.lrs-s-appointments-clause: The Court divided over whether the appointing authority qualified as a court of law or a department head.

learning.separateOpinions: Nine to zero on the judgment. Justice Scalia, joined by Justices O'Connor, Kennedy and Souter, concurred in part and concurred in the judgment. He agreed that special trial judges are inferior officers and that the assignment was authorized, but he read Courts of Law to mean only Article III courts and concluded instead that the Tax Court is a Department whose Chief Judge is its head, so the appointment was valid on that ground.
